summary: Describes the binding protocols used with ONC RPC version 2, which help clients find the right service on a server. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: A way to find out which door to knock on to reach a particular service on another computer.

questions: how does onc rpc binding work
what is a universal address in onc rpc
subtitle: How an ONC RPC client finds which transport address a server program is listening on, using one well-known lookup service on port 111.

tldr.problem: An RPC client knows a program number and version, but the TCP or UDP port a server uses is usually picked dynamically, and well-known ports are too few for the many possible services.
tldr.mechanism: Every server registers with a lookup service, RPC program 100000 on port 111 over TCP and UDP, and clients ask it for the address. RPCBIND (versions 3 and 4) uses transport-independent universal addresses; the older Port Mapper (version 2) handles TCP and UDP ports directly.
tldr.outcome: Only one fixed port is needed to reach any registered RPC service. RFC 1833 is a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 5665.

today: RFC 1833 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 5665; it has not been obsoleted. It is the specification of RPCBIND versions 3 and 4 and the Port Mapper version 2.

sections.title: Why RPC Needs a Lookup Service
sections.content:
An RPC service is identified by its program number, its version number, and a transport address. For TCP/IP or UDP/IP the transport address is an IP address plus a TCP or UDP port number. Program and version numbers are normally built into the client. The network address usually comes from a name service or is given to the client as a parameter.

The port is the awkward part. It is usually determined dynamically and varies with each invocation of the service. Well-known ports are a small range for some transports, while the number of services is potentially very large. So servers register their address with one well-known lookup service, and clients ask that service where to go.

RFC 1833 describes three versions of this lookup service. All use RPC program number 100000 and port 111 over TCP and UDP. Versions 3 and 4 are RPCBIND; version 2 is the Port Mapper. Readers are expected to know ONC RPC version 2 (RFC 1831) and XDR (RFC 1832).
sections.eli5: Services move to a different door each time they start. So there is one front desk that never moves, and everyone asks it which door to use.

sections.title: RPCBIND: Universal Addresses
sections.content:
The RPCBIND program maps RPC program and version numbers to universal addresses. It sits at a well-known address on each supported transport, and other programs register their dynamically allocated address with it.

A universal address is an ASCII string form of the transport-dependent address. The string format for each transport is defined by that transport's addressing authority. This makes RPCBIND usable for binding RPC clients and servers over any transport, not only TCP and UDP.

Each registration is an rpcb record holding the program number (r_prog), version (r_vers), network id (r_netid), universal address (r_addr) and owner (r_owner). The network id is a local name chosen by the system administrator and cannot be relied on to have the same value on every system.

RPCBIND also supports broadcast RPC. A program has different addresses on different machines, so a client cannot broadcast to it directly. Instead the client sends its message to the RPCBIND program at the broadcast address. Each RPCBIND instance that receives it calls the local service, then sends the reply back to the client.
sections.eli5: Instead of a house number that only works in one town, the new desk writes any address down as plain text, so it works for any kind of network. To reach everyone at once, you shout at all the desks and each one knocks on its own building's door.

sections.title: RPCBIND Procedures, Versions 3 and 4
sections.content:
Version 3 defines eight procedures. A service registers with RPCBPROC_SET when it starts, and removes itself with RPCBPROC_UNSET when it goes away. SET refuses to create a mapping if one already exists for (r_prog, r_vers, r_netid). Only the owner of the service or the super-user may unset it.

RPCBPROC_GETADDR returns the universal address where a program is awaiting calls. The r_netid in the argument is ignored and is inferred from the transport the request came in on. RPCBPROC_DUMP lists the whole database. RPCBPROC_GETTIME returns the local time in seconds since midnight, 1 January 1970. RPCBPROC_UADDR2TADDR and RPCBPROC_TADDR2UADDR convert between universal and transport-specific addresses. RPCBPROC_CALLIT calls another procedure on the same machine without knowing its address, and answers only if the call succeeded.

Version 4 keeps all of these and adds more. RPCBPROC_BCAST is the same as CALLIT, renamed to show it is for broadcast. RPCBPROC_INDIRECT is similar but returns an error indication instead of staying silent, and should not be used for broadcast. RPCBPROC_GETVERSADDR returns an address only for the exact version asked for. RPCBPROC_GETADDRLIST returns a list of addresses, which may reveal alternate transports. RPCBPROC_GETSTAT returns statistics on requests received.

All procedures except SET and UNSET can be called by clients on other machines. RPCBIND accepts SET and UNSET only from clients on the same machine.
sections.eli5: A service tells the desk where it lives when it opens and takes its name off when it closes. Anyone can ask the desk where a service is, but only a service on the same computer can change the list.

sections.title: The Port Mapper, Version 2
sections.content:
The Port Mapper is the older protocol. It maps program and version numbers directly to TCP or UDP port numbers, so unlike RPCBIND it is transport specific. It is contacted on port 111 over either UDP or TCP.

A mapping is a (prog, vers, prot, port) record, where prot is 6 for TCP or 17 for UDP. The procedures are PMAPPROC_NULL (procedure 0, which does no work), PMAPPROC_SET, PMAPPROC_UNSET, PMAPPROC_GETPORT, PMAPPROC_DUMP and PMAPPROC_CALLIT.

GETPORT takes a program, version and protocol and returns the port. A port of zero means the program has not been registered. For UNSET, the protocol and port fields of the argument are ignored. CALLIT only replies if the called procedure succeeded, and the port mapper talks to the remote program over UDP only.
sections.eli5: The old desk only understands one kind of address, the TCP and UDP port numbers. If it cannot find your service it answers with zero, which means not registered.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo. The one access rule it states is operational: RPCBIND accepts registration and removal requests (SET and UNSET) only from clients on the same machine.
sections.eli5: The memo does not talk about safety. It only says that just programs on the same computer may change the desk's list.
